Kafka consumer services may appear in the discovered graph, but they are not required members of any $T(u)$, so asynchronous semantics can matter

We omit Monte Carlo error bars: with $M{=}5\times 10^{6}$ trials per job and averaging over 50 jobs, their contribution is below the plot resolution.

At low failure fractions ($p_{\mathrm{fail}}{=}0.1$ and $0.3$) the model is optimistic (roughly +10 and +5 percentage points).
At $p_{\mathrm{fail}}{=}0.5$ the aggregate estimate is close to unbiased, while at higher failure fractions it becomes pessimistic (about $-4$ points at $0.7$ and $-12$ points at $0.9$).
Overall, the trace-discovered connectivity model captures the degradation trend but omits mechanisms (e.g., retries and gray failures) that shape behaviour at the extremes.

The two semantics are indistinguishable at the aggregate level: values for $\hat{R}^{(\mathrm{all})}$ and $\hat{R}^{(\mathrm{async})}$ match to three decimals across all $p_{\mathrm{fail}}$.
For these predicates, discounting Kafka edges does not change reachability to the synchronous targets that define immediate success.

\subsection{Endpoint-Level Effect of Async Semantics (RQ2)}

To isolate the effect of asynchronous semantics we examine
$\Delta_u(p_{\mathrm{fail}})=\hat{R}^{(\mathrm{async})}_u-\hat{R}^{(\mathrm{all})}_u$.
Across all endpoints and failure fractions, $|\Delta_u|$ stays around $10^{-5}$ and fluctuates near zero (Fig.~\ref{fig:results}b).
This is far below the practical threshold $\Delta_{\min}{=}0.01$ and below the resolution of the live measurements, so treating Kafka edges as non-blocking does not change conclusions for immediate HTTP success on this demo.

The reason is structural: the discovered Kafka edges connect producers to downstream consumers that process events after the HTTP response returns, and those consumer services are not required by the target sets in Table~\ref{tab:endpoints}.
If ``success'' instead required end-to-end completion of the asynchronous workflow, Kafka reachability (and richer broker semantics) would become central.

\textbf{RQ1.} The trace-derived connectivity model reproduces the overall degradation trend but is optimistic at low failure fractions and pessimistic when most services are down.

\textbf{RQ2.} For the studied endpoints, the async treatment changes predicted availability by at most $10^{-5}$ (0.001 percentage points), yielding no measurable benefit for immediate-response success.

\textbf{RQ3.} The bias pattern matches our prior DeathStarBench results~\cite{krasnovsky2025modeldiscovery,gan2019deathstarbench}; a connectivity-only model is a reasonable baseline for immediate-response SLOs, while richer semantics are warranted when success depends on eventual processing or when additional failure modes dominate.
